statement: In how many different orders can four people stand in a queue?

choices.misconception: I multiplied four by itself, which would allow the same person to fill two positions.
I multiplied four by three and stopped before placing the last two people.
I counted the people rather than the arrangements of them.
I doubled the number of people, as though each one simply had two options.

hints: Fill the positions one at a time and count the choices left.
The first position has four candidates, the second three, and so on, because each person placed is no longer available. Multiply those shrinking counts together.
4 x 3 x 2 x 1 counts the queues, since every placement removes one person from the pool.

solutions.reliable: Fill the queue from the front: 4 choices, then 3, then 2, then 1, giving 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24. The transferable idea: arrangements multiply shrinking counts, whereas repeated independent choices multiply the same count, and confusing the two produces the 16 on offer.

whyOnTest: Arrangements and repeated choices look identical in words and differ in arithmetic, so both answers sit side by side in the choices.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
